decision: lab-agent is delivered by the package conveyor (linux-package-distribution-oco/conveyor@v1); it keeps only its declaration, build scripts, PKGBUILD, public key and install test.
why: Its delivery workflows were a near copy of snapall's; copies drift and fixes do not travel.
rejected: Keeping its own copy of the delivery machinery.

decision: lab-agent records each wait itself - start, end, what is waited on, the project - and requires both on a waiting submit; a gatherer brings the waits into each project's data.
why: Capture must be unavoidable and cost nothing: the place every wait happens is lab-agent's own wait.
rejected: Logging waits by hand (it would be skipped); estimating them afterwards.

decision: Every process a job starts carries the job's mark in its environment (OCO_AGENT_JOB). When the job ends, overstays, or was left by a run that died, everything carrying its mark is ended - asked to stop first, then made to. Something meant to outlive a job is started as a service, not as its child.
why: Crash-only cleanup must not trust the runner to have lived: a dead run's jobs are found by their mark and cleared before anything else happens. The mark reaches children's children, which nothing else here does.
rejected: Process groups (a child can leave its group); a death signal to children (it reaches only the direct child); systemd's control group alone (tests, and machines without it, would have nothing; it still helps where present).

decision: Work is asked for through the jobs repository as files under oco-agent/jobs - apart from lab-agent's jobs/, so during the switch neither agent takes the other's work. A file's top line says who asked, when and its limits, and counts only at the top. When work was asked comes from the asking, never from when it is read. Drivers' beats are the repository's Actions variables. Only oco-agent-github knows GitHub.
why: An agent that was down must not see old work as new: the asking's own time makes such work expire instead of run (the quieter cousin of the 2026-11-11 replay). A header read anywhere is how lab-agent's client lost a line from inside a script. A beat every few minutes as a commit would fill the history with hundreds of meaningless commits a day.
rejected: Taking the moment of reading as the moment of asking; a header read anywhere in the script; a separate metadata file beside each script (two writes, and a window with one but not the other); beats as commits; a second repository for oco-agent's jobs (the same trust and the same token, twice the setup).

decision: oco-agent is built inside lab-agent's repository (oco-agent/), tested by its CI and kept out of its releases, until it takes over and the repository takes its name.
why: Its design, research and backlog already live here; lab-agent must keep serving while it is proven; tad's Rust version grew the same way.
rejected: A new repository now (the reasoning and the code would live apart, and the history would split).

decision: Each driver - a person or a machine - has a lease of its own, kept alive by its beats: a job starts only while the driver who asked for it is still there. Beats are what is known now, not a history: one fact per driver, a newer beat replacing an older and never the reverse; they are kept apart from the journal, behind their own port, with their own check in the measure.
why: oco-agent coordinates work for any driver; one driver going silent must not stop another's work, and must stop its own. Beats arrive often and only the latest matters, so they are state, where the journal is history.
rejected: One lease for 'the' driver (the first design: a silent AI would have stopped the author's work too); beats as journal entries (hundreds of lines a day that say nothing after the next one).

decision: The redesigned lab-agent is oco-agent: born beside lab-agent, which serves until the switch - as tad's Rust version grew beside the Python one - then lab-agent retires.
why: The author, 2026-11-12: it is tied to ocoeco by design. 'agent' is the established word for this role; 'oco-' names its family and its dependency on ocoeco.
rejected: runner (GitHub's word - true, but it says nothing of the voice, the journal or the leases); keeping lab-agent (it names a place, not what it belongs to); renaming in place (the old one must keep serving until the new one is proven).

decision: lab-agent's core speaks its own language and depends on nothing outside itself (a crate with no input or output); every technology - git and GitHub, ntfy, systemd - is an adapter behind a port the core defines, and its words appear nowhere above it; areas are named for what lab-agent is for; the playbook's guards check it on every change; in-memory adapters run the chaos tests. The journal is declared tad tables queried with SQL, and where they live is itself an adapter; finished work becomes glimpses. The journal's SQL is tad's, and tad's SQL is DuckDB's (tad-engine 2026-11-12-sql-is-duckdb), as tad's original research decided.
why: The author, 2026-11-12: follow the ideal-project guidelines; the implementation must not rely on GitHub - it is today's adapter, and switching it (to Redis, say) must be a clean replacement; git as a heap of files is a one-off mess when tad is a database and ocoeco makes every action intelligible.
rejected: A core that calls GitHub and git directly (the prototype's way, and the root of the incident's reach); folders named ports and adapters (the playbook: names say what the program is for); the journal as files in a repository with no declaration.

decision: oco-agent is trusted with nothing until it has watched lab-agent: a shadow run reads lab-agent's newest log every ten minutes through oco-agent's rules, keeps its own journal, and alerts urgently when lab-agent starts work oco-agent would have refused. It decides; it never acts.
why: Rules proven on tests and on one night's log should also hold on the days that follow, before they run anything; and lab-agent is still the one running jobs, so a replay there must be noticed at once.
rejected: Switching to oco-agent at once (proven only on the past); a daily report (a replay storm ran 102 jobs in twenty minutes on 2026-11-11).

decision: What happened is spoken back to the repository work was asked through, on a branch of its own (spoken): the journal, and each job's log. It is written only when something changed - the journal at most every ten seconds, a running job's log at most every minute, a finished job's log at once - logs before the journal, so a driver who reads that a job ended finds its log there. Only jobs the running agent did are spoken. A driver anywhere uses standing, log and wait with --via; waiting is a beat, and wait's exit status says how the job ended (0 finished, 1 failed, 124 out of time, 3 expired, 4 parked, 2 not ended yet).
why: A driver must see how work went from wherever it drives, as with lab-agent's results - but in the one repository it asked through. The history of asking stays readable on main. Writing only on change keeps within GitHub's limits on content creation as well as its hourly budget.
rejected: A second repository for results, as lab-agent has (two places for a driver to look, twice the setup); writing on main (the asking history drowned in reports); writing every change at once (commits by the second); speaking every log in the folder when a runner starts (a burst after each restart).

decision: Everything that polls GitHub asks conditionally (ETag), so an unchanged answer costs nothing; oco-agent reads what is left of the hour's budget from every answer and, below 500, takes work in only every 2 minutes, saying so once. Writing - commits, variables - happens only when something changed.
why: The 5,000-an-hour budget is shared by everything on the account; one careless poller can starve land, the client and the pin updater together. lab-agent had learned this; the redesign must carry it over, not lose it.
rejected: Polling without conditions (about 480 an hour for intake alone); a fixed slower interval (slow even when the budget is plentiful); a second account or token for the agent (two secrets to keep and rotate, and the token is to be rotated already).

decision: oco-agent does work through Hands - start, look, stop, clear - whatever actually runs a job (processes on this machine today). A job is claimed in the journal before it starts, and does not start if the claim is refused; its end is written as it happens, and an end that could not be written is kept and written at the next step. Each job says how long it may run and is stopped if it overstays. A run of the agent is numbered by the moment it began, to the millisecond.
why: The replay of 2026-11-11 came from work whose record lived apart from the doing; here nothing starts unrecorded. Deciding needs only that no two runs share a number, so a moment serves where a counter would be more state to keep right.
rejected: Starting first and writing after (a crash between the two leaves a job run and unrecorded); a counter of runs kept on disk; retrying a job that could not start (it would fail the same way, repeatedly).

decision: lab-agent is redesigned around a journal per job, run-once by construction, the driver's lease with park-on-silence, each job's heartbeat, flows of idempotent steps that resume, a working tree per job and side-by-side by resource, crash-only recovery, a watcher outside the machine, secrets kept out of URLs, and its data flowing through ocoeco - in five stages, each proven by chaos tests before the next (DESIGN.md). Refined the same day by 2026-11-12-ports-names-and-tables: ports and adapters with the playbook's names and guards, and the journal as tad tables queried with SQL.
why: The 2026-11-11 incident traced to a foundation laid as a one-off prototype; the author asked for the best the world has learned, with the full picture in mind.
rejected: Patching the replay and carrying on (the other paths stay open); adopting a durable-execution engine such as Temporal or Restate (a server to run and secure on one machine with no inbound port - lab-agent takes their proven ideas into a small core instead, with git as the record it already has).
sources: temporal-durable-execution, kleppmann-locking, healthchecks, crash-only, k8s-jobs, idempotency-keys

decision: The lab is watched from outside by probing it: a workflow in the jobs repository asks a tiny job every half hour and alerts the urgent channel itself - once - when the lab has not answered for 45 minutes; it says so when the lab answers again, and asks no new probe while one is unanswered. It needs no secret beyond the channels: the probe writes its answer back into the same repository with the lab's own token.
why: On 2026-11-11 the agent stalled while the machine was on, and the only alert path ran through the agent. A beat from a timer would have stayed happy through the stall; only work actually done proves the agent takes work (black-box probing). Watching from GitHub keeps the alert independent of the lab.
rejected: A timer on the lab sending beats (blind to an agent that stalls while the machine runs); a hosted dead man's switch such as Healthchecks (one more account, and still fed by the lab); a probe every few minutes (noise in the jobs repository, and a long job would look like silence).
